Examples of trial-type, evidentiary hearings that are not conducted 
under the APA’s formal hearing provisions are legion and include the 
adjudication of:
• 
Deportation and asylum claims by the Office of Immigration 
Review (within the Department of Justice);
• 
Inter partes challenges to the validity of previously issued 
patents by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board of the Patent 
and Trademark Office (within the Department of Commfirce);
• 
Contract disputes between private contractors and executive 
agencies by the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals (within 
the General Services Administration (GSA));
• 
Debarment and suspension of private parties from ent Ari ng 
into procurement contracts with the government by twenty- 
four agencies across government under the Federal 
Acquisition Regulation, adopted by GSA pursuant to 
statutory authority;
• 
Minor civil penalties and the issuance, modification, 
reissuance, and revocation of various environm Antal permits 
by the Environmental Protection Agency; and
• 
Employment discrimination claims by federal employees 
against their employing agencies by the Equal Employment 
Opportunity Commission (EEOC) (these hearings are 
required by the EEOC’s own regulations and not by the 
apphcable statutes).

Informal, trial-type hearings have many things in common with formal 
APA hearings. They typically are conducted according to detailed procedural 
rules, which may include many of the procedures required by the APA. A set 
of recommendations adopted by the Administrative Conference of the United 
States (“ACUS”), identify best practices that are meant to balance accuracy, 
efficiency, and fairness in the procedures used for such hearings. 
Administrative Conference Recommendation 2016—4, “Evidentiary Hearings 
Not Required by the Administrative Procedure Act” (Dec. 13, 2016). The 
recommendations include requirements that decisions be based on an exclusive 
record with no ex parte communications outside the record; that decisional and 
adversarial personnel be separated; and that decisionmakers be disqualified 
for confiicts of interest or bias. They also include suggestions for allowing
